title: Nachmanides' other way
hook: a more mystical approach to the same texts

segments.voice: Yesterday, controversy: Maimonides accused, critiqued in the margin, banned, and then read at the center. Your line: controversy, then canon. Today, a rival who argued with him by name.

A hot afternoon. Abraham sits at the opening of his tent, looks up, and sees three men standing nearby. He runs to meet them, bows, and hurries Sarah to bake bread while he picks out a calf. A homely scene from Genesis. Now hand it to two great rabbis named Moses. One says it all happened in a prophetic vision. The other says those words contradict Scripture. Same text, same tent, two very different readings.
screen: `THREE MEN AT THE TENT.` → `A VISION?` → `OR SOMETHING ELSE?`

segments.voice: Nachmanides' other way. His name was Rabbi Moses ben Nachman, known as the Ramban, from Girona, in Catalonia. First, he argues out loud. In the Guide, Maimonides reads the three men as something Abraham saw in a prophetic vision. In his commentary on Genesis, the Ramban quotes him, then pushes back hard: these words, he says, contradict Scripture, and one shouldn't listen to them. If it was only a vision, why the bread, the calf, the hurrying? He reads the visitors as real messengers, seen in a form people could see. Second, the offerings. Maimonides explains the sacrifices as a gentle step: people in the ancient world knew worship by offerings, so the Torah kept the form and turned it toward God alone. The Ramban objects. The Torah calls an offering "of a sweet savour unto the LORD." He sees in it a picture for the one who brings it: what is done to the animal should make the person think, this should have been me, and the offering stands in their place. Third, the way of truth. The Ramban drops a short hint and says the meaning is known by the way of truth, pointing to a hidden, mystical layer of the Torah, the tradition known as Kabbalah. He hints. He doesn't spell it out. Fourth, two ways, one Torah. Maimonides reaches for reason and philosophy; the Ramban, for the plain story and for hidden depths. Both read the same verses seriously. Students still open both, side by side, and learn from the argument.
screen: `HE ARGUES OUT LOUD.` · `A SWEET SAVOUR UNTO THE LORD.` · `THE WAY OF TRUTH.` · `TWO WAYS, ONE TORAH.` · then, large: `TWO WAYS OF THINKING.`

segments.voice: Pick one question that matters to you, like why people suffer or why pray, and give it two readers: one who answers with careful reasons, step by step, and one who answers with a story, or a sense that something deeper is hidden there. Let each speak for a few breaths without interrupting. You don't have to choose a winner; just notice what each one sees that the other misses.
Nachmanides' other way. The Ramban's reading of the Torah: close to the plain story, open to a hidden way of truth, and willing to argue with Maimonides by name. Today's word.
Your line: two ways of thinking. One Torah can hold both readers. That's day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: The Ramban's Torah commentary is printed in standard rabbinic Bibles, and students often read it alongside other commentators, comparing how each one reads the same verse.

chat.says: Did the big medieval rabbis basically agree on what the Torah means?
options: Not always. The Ramban argued with Maimonides by name, and students still read both.
Yes. The Ramban just repeated Maimonides and never disagreed with him.
No, and the Ramban's side won, so Maimonides is no longer studied.
chat.meaning: The Ramban quoted the Guide and pushed back on the three visitors and on the offerings; both men's books are still read side by side.

notes: Ramban on Genesis 18:1 paraphrased: he cites Guide 2:42 and says such words contradict Scripture and it is forbidden to listen to them (stronger: 'all the more so to believe them'). Softened to 'one shouldn't listen to them'. Please confirm.
Ramban's reading of the visitors ('real messengers, seen in a form people could see') is a simplification of his discussion of angels appearing in human form and of 'clothed' sight; please check.

Ramban on Leviticus 1:9 paraphrased: the one bringing the offering should feel that what is done to the animal ought to have been done to him, and the offering is a substitute; and his objection to Guide 3:32. Please confirm.
Leviticus 1:9 JPS 1917: confirm 'of a sweet savour unto the LORD' (JPS 1917 'an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the LORD').
'the tradition that would come to be called Kabbalah' and the characterization of 'al derekh ha-emet as kabbalistic allusion: please confirm phrasing for this path; day 1171 introduces Kabbalah.
'Students still open both, side by side' kept general; howItsDone says the Ramban is printed in standard rabbinic Bibles (Mikraot Gedolot). Please confirm.
